episodes.title: Einstein's Special Relativity: Two Postulates Reshape Reality
episodes.summary: This episode explores Einstein's 1905 paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies, examining how two simple postulates—the relativity of inertial frames and the constancy of light speed—lead to counterintuitive consequences like time dilation, length contraction, and the equivalence of mass and energy. Ideal for anyone seeking to understand the conceptual foundations of special relativity beyond equations.

episodes.file_title: Great Papers 02 How Black Holes Radiate, Hawking 1975
episodes.title: Hawking Radiation: Black Holes Glow and Evaporate
episodes.summary: This episode explores Hawking's 1974 discovery that black holes emit thermal radiation and gradually evaporate, resolving a paradox between general relativity and thermodynamics. It covers the classical black hole, the area theorem, Bekenstein entropy, quantum field theory in curved spacetime, and the information paradox. Suited for physicists and advanced students interested in black hole thermodynamics and quantum gravity.

episodes.file_title: Great Papers 03 The Double Helix, Watson and Crick 1953
episodes.title: Watson and Crick's Double Helix: Structure Solves Heredity
episodes.summary: This episode traces how Watson and Crick solved the structure of DNA in 1953 by synthesizing three key clues: the chemical composition of bases, Chargaff's pairing rules, and Franklin's X-ray crystallography evidence. The speakers explain how the double helix structure elegantly solves two biological problems simultaneously—information storage and faithful copying—through complementary base pairing. The episode suits anyone interested in how a single structural insight revolutionized molecular biology and enabled modern genetics.

episodes.file_title: Great Papers 04 Shannon and the Birth of Information, 1948
episodes.title: Shannon's Mathematical Theory of Communication, 1948
episodes.summary: This episode explores Claude Shannon's foundational 1948 paper that quantified information through the concepts of bits and entropy, establishing the mathematical framework for all digital communication. It covers how Shannon unified telegraph, telephone, and radio engineering by treating information as measurable uncertainty rather than meaning. The episode suits anyone interested in the origins of information theory, digital technology, data compression, error correction, and the deep mathematical principles underlying modern communication systems.

episodes.file_title: Great Papers 05 Attention Is All You Need, 2017
episodes.title: Attention Is All You Need: The Transformer Architecture
episodes.summary: This episode explores the 2017 Google paper that introduced the Transformer architecture, replacing sequential recurrent neural networks with pure attention mechanisms. It explains how attention allows parallel processing of language by letting each word query all others simultaneously, eliminating distance-based degradation. The episode suits anyone interested in understanding the foundational architecture behind modern large language models.

episodes.title: Einstein's General Relativity: Gravity as Curved Spacetime
episodes.summary: This episode traces Einstein's 1915 theory of general relativity, starting from loose threads in special relativity and culminating in the field equations that describe gravity as spacetime curvature rather than force. It covers the equivalence principle, the metric tensor, and three experimental confirmations including Mercury's orbit precession, starlight bending, and gravitational waves. Ideal for those seeking to understand how Einstein unified gravity with relativity and the experimental evidence supporting the theory.

episodes.file_title: Great Papers 07 On Computable Numbers, Turing 1936
episodes.title: Turing's Computable Numbers: Machines, Logic, and Limits
episodes.summary: This episode explores Turing's 1936 paper on computable numbers, which introduced the theoretical machine that became the blueprint for all modern computers. It covers how Turing formalized the concept of mechanical computation to address Hilbert's foundational program in mathematics, and demonstrates fundamental limits on what machines can compute. Suited for those interested in computability theory, mathematical logic, and the theoretical foundations of computing.
